line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3
teaches: When your centre is attacked, defending it with a pawn is not the only answer — and it is often the worst one, because the propping move develops nothing and commits a square your pieces wanted. Give the pawn up and DEVELOP instead: a lead in development buys back more than one pawn is worth.
explains: The bishop takes the strongest diagonal it has, pointing at h7 and covering the light squares in front of the centre. The pawn in the middle can be taken; the position it is being traded for is a full move ahead in development.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O f6 Re1
teaches: When the opponent strikes at the pawn that anchors your whole position, capturing back is the move that throws the position away — the pawn is not the point, the square it sits on is, and taking removes your own occupant of it. Add a defender instead and make them do the trading.
explains: The rook comes to e1 straight behind the advanced pawn, holding it and holding the file behind it. If the pawn is captured now, a piece of ours arrives on that square rather than the position simply opening.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O f6 Re1 fxe5 Nxe5 Nf6 Bf4
teaches: A pin is attractive because it is concrete, and that is exactly why it distracts — if your position is built around holding one square, judge every developing move by whether it adds a guard to that square, because the flashier square that pins a knight but abandons the outpost is a worse move even though it looks like it does more.
explains: The bishop settles on f4, defending the knight that occupies the key square. The pin one square further along looks more active and touches nothing that matters here; this is the square that keeps the knight where it is.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 cxd4 O-O f6 Re1 fxe5 Nxe5 Nf6 Bf4 Bd6 Nd2
teaches: When a piece must be developed and a square must be reinforced, look for the move that does both — a knight has more than one route out, and the route that passes through a square from which it will defend your outpost is worth more than the one that merely looks central.
explains: The knight comes to d2, covering f3 — the square from which it will add another defender to the outpost — and holding e4 on the way. Nothing has been developed for its own sake.
